deck_name: Tarocchino di Bologna — The Real 62-Card Bolognese Deck

trump-matto.name: The Fool
trump-matto.Scene: Il Matto is rendered in the double-ended format standard to Bolognese court cards — a jester figure in patchwork multi-colored clothing and a feathered cap occupies both halves of the card, one right-side up and one inverted. The costume of the Fool is vivid and festive, a patchwork of red, blue, and yellow. This fool is not a vagabond with a bundle but a court jester, suggesting the Bolognese association of the Fool with the carnival figure of professional festivity.

trump-bagatto.name: The Magician
trump-bagatto.Scene: Il Bagatto (the Conjurer or Mountebank) appears in the double-ended format with a figure in a low-crowned hat standing at a table. Flanking figures at either end of the card suggest the carnival or street-performance context of the Bolognese Bagatto. Where the Marseille Bateleur is a solitary tradesman behind his paraphernalia, the Bolognese card embeds him in a scene with attendants or audience, consistent with the conjurer as social performer.

trump-papa-a.name: Papa (Moor) I
trump-papa-a.Scene: The first of four Papi (Moors) who replace the standard trumps II through V in the Bolognese deck. This Moor figure wears a jester's pointed cap in bright colors and holds a long lance or staff. Like all four Papi, he is rendered in the double-ended format with his image mirrored at top and bottom. The Papi Mori replaced the Papessa, Empress, Emperor, and Pope to avoid religious and political controversy, substituting secular court figures for sacred ones.

trump-papa-b.name: Papa (Moor) II
trump-papa-b.Scene: The second Papa Moro, rendered in double-ended format. This figure wears a simpler or different colored costume than the first, holding a long lance or spear. The four Papi together form a group of interchangeable but visually distinct Moorish figures, each carrying a lance and dressed in colorful Bolognese court style.

trump-papa-c.name: Papa (Moor) III
trump-papa-c.Scene: The third Papa Moro, double-ended, in colorful doublet and without the pointed hat of the first Moor. This figure has a slightly different posture and costume detail from the others in the set, distinguishing him within the quartet while maintaining the overall Moorish character. The lance or staff remains the consistent attribute across all four Papi.

trump-papa-d.name: Papa (Moor) IV
trump-papa-d.Scene: The fourth and final Papa Moro, double-ended, appears in green and red costume with a leaf or floral crown and a raised or open hand. This figure is the most plainly dressed of the four, his raised hand suggesting a gesture of greeting or blessing — a secular echo of the Pope's benediction that this figure has replaced in the Bolognese deck.

trump-amore.name: Love
trump-amore.Scene: L'Amore (Love) shows the conventional Lovers scene — figures beneath a winged Cupid or amorous arrangement — in the Bolognese trump order at position VI. The Bolognese Amore follows the Italian tradition of the Trionfi sequence, placing the triumph of Love early in the hierarchical sequence after the secular substitutes for religious authority.

trump-carro.name: The Chariot
trump-carro.Scene: Il Carro (The Chariot) appears at position VII in the Bolognese order, showing the conventional triumph of the vehicle of power — a crowned or helmeted figure riding in a chariot. In the Italian Trionfi tradition the chariot represents the martial triumph, the military procession that Petrarch placed in his allegorical sequence of ascending victories.

trump-temperanza.name: Temperance
trump-temperanza.Scene: La Temperanza (Temperance) appears at position VIII in the Bolognese trump sequence — an earlier position than in the Marseille tradition, where Temperance typically appears at XIV. The Bolognese ordering places the temperate virtue of moderation and measured pouring directly after the Chariot's triumph. The card shows the conventional figure of Temperance with two vessels, pouring liquid from one to the other.

trump-giustizia.name: Justice
trump-giustizia.Scene: La Giustizia (Justice) appears at position VIIII in the Bolognese sequence, showing the conventional crowned or winged female figure with sword and scales. Justice in the Bolognese tarocchino follows the conventional personification of equity and measure, the allegorical tribunal that sits over the card's triumphal procession.

trump-forza.name: Strength
trump-forza.Scene: La Forza (Strength) appears at position X in the Bolognese sequence, showing the conventional figure of Force — a person subduing a lion, typically a woman opening or closing the animal's mouth. The Bolognese Strength follows the standard Italian iconography of this virtue without the dramatic departures seen in some French decks.

trump-ruota.name: Wheel of Fortune
trump-ruota.Scene: La Ruota (The Wheel of Fortune) appears at position XI in the Bolognese sequence. The wheel with its ascending and descending figures — the crowned figure at the apex and the fallen ones below — represents Fortune's indifference. In the Bolognese ordering the Wheel sits mid-sequence between Strength and the Old Man, embedded in the cascade of allegorical triumphs.

trump-vecchio.name: The Old Man (Time)
trump-vecchio.Scene: Il Vecchio (The Old Man) appears at position XII in the Bolognese sequence, replacing the Hermit (L'Hermite) of the Marseille tradition. Where the Hermit carries a lantern, the Bolognese Old Man is sometimes depicted as Father Time with an hourglass, emphasizing temporality and the passage of years rather than the search for inner light. He represents the triumph of Time over earthly power.

trump-traditore.name: The Traitor (Hanged Man)
trump-traditore.Scene: Il Traditore (The Traitor) appears at position XIII in the Bolognese sequence, the Bolognese name for the card known in other traditions as the Hanged Man (Il Penduto). The term 'Traitor' emphasizes the judicial nature of the suspension — in Renaissance Italy, traitors were hung by one foot as a mark of shame, making this punishment iconography more explicit in the Bolognese naming.

trump-morte.name: Death
trump-morte.Scene: La Morte (Death) appears at position XIIII in the Bolognese sequence, following the Traitor. Death's skeleton with scythe mows the field of the living in the conventional Trionfi tradition. The Bolognese Death card follows the Italian iconographic convention of the skeleton as universal harvester, the triumph of mortality that follows upon betrayal and judgment.

trump-diavolo.name: The Devil
trump-diavolo.Scene: Il Diavolo (The Devil) appears at position XV in the Bolognese sequence, following Death. The Devil's throne or pedestal with bound figures — the conventional tableau of demonic bondage — represents the triumph of spiritual peril in the allegorical sequence. The Bolognese Devil follows the standard Italian iconography without the wild departures of some northern European decks.

trump-torre.name: The Lightning (Tower)
trump-torre.Scene: La Torre (The Tower) appears at position XVI in the Bolognese sequence, showing the conventional lightning-struck tower with figures falling. In the Italian tradition this card is often called 'Il Fulmine' (The Lightning) or 'La Saetta' (The Arrow/Bolt), emphasizing the celestial strike rather than the architectural ruin. The Bolognese Tower follows the standard Italian iconography of catastrophic celestial rupture.

trump-stella.name: The Star
trump-stella.Scene: La Stella (The Star) appears at position XVII in the Bolognese sequence. The conventional Star shows a figure pouring water beneath a sky of stars — the Italian Star typically follows the Marseille iconographic type more closely than some French variants. The star card in the tarocchino represents celestial guidance in the sequence that ascends through Moon and Sun toward the World and Angel.

trump-luna.name: The Moon
trump-luna.Scene: La Luna (The Moon) appears at position XVIII in a format distinctive to the Bolognese tradition. The double-ended card shows two identical female figures standing facing inward toward a large round moon face at center, with stars scattered around. The bilateral symmetry of the two figures flanking the central moon is characteristic of the Bolognese lunar card, entirely different from the Marseille type with dogs, towers, and a pool.

trump-sole.name: The Sun
trump-sole.Scene: Il Sole (The Sun) appears at position XVIIII in the distinctive Bolognese format. Three sun faces with radiating rays appear in the double-ended composition — a central rider or figure on horseback holds a whip or flag between two sun faces, one above and one below. The three-sun arrangement with the central rider is one of the most iconographically distinctive features of the Bolognese tarocchino.

trump-mondo.name: The World
trump-mondo.Scene: Il Mondo (The World) appears at position XX in the Bolognese sequence — one position earlier than in standard tarot, where the World is typically the last numbered trump. The double-ended card shows two jester or court figures in colorful costumes standing at either end, flanking a large dark globe or sphere at the center that bears a cross or geometric pattern. This is entirely distinct from the Marseille dancer-in-wreath and represents the world as a globe held between two figures.

trump-angelo.name: The Angel (Judgement)
trump-angelo.Scene: L'Angelo (The Angel) appears at position XXI — the highest numbered trump in the Bolognese sequence, where standard tarot places it at XX. The double-ended card shows a winged angel figure in symmetrical format, trumpeting or blessing from the card's center. The Bolognese reversal of Mondo (XX) and Angelo (XXI) places divine judgment above worldly completion, the angel having the final word in the hierarchical ascent.

coins-ace.name: Ace of Coins
coins-ace.Scene: The Ace of Coins (Denari) shows a large decorative cartouche or oval bordered by small floral and geometric elements. A central circular coin ring surrounds a manufacturer's inscription — in Bolognese tradition the ace of coins is the card on which the card-maker places their mark or license seal. The overall effect is ornate and heraldic, the single coin rendered as a cartouche of civic and commercial authority.

coins-six.name: Six of Coins
coins-six.Scene: The Six of Coins shows six circular starburst coins arranged in two columns of three against a white background. Each coin bears a red starburst or sunflower design on a gold ground, the Italian denaro pip in its clean, direct Bolognese rendering. The six-coin card is open and symmetrical, the suit's ornamental pip displayed without additional embellishment.

coins-seven.name: Seven of Coins
coins-seven.Scene: The Seven of Coins shows seven circular starburst coins in the conventional Italian pip arrangement — typically a four-two-one or three-one-three distribution that accommodates the odd count. Each coin bears the characteristic starburst design of the Bolognese denari suit. The seven-coin card has a slight asymmetry that marks it as an odd-number pip.

coins-eight.name: Eight of Coins
coins-eight.Scene: The Eight of Coins shows eight circular starburst coins in a symmetrical pip arrangement. The even number allows a balanced four-by-two or two-column distribution, the eight Bolognese denari in their clean Italian pip style against a white background.

coins-nine.name: Nine of Coins
coins-nine.Scene: The Nine of Coins shows nine circular starburst coins approaching the density of the ten. The nine Bolognese denari are distributed across the card in the standard Italian pip convention, the suit nearing its maximum pip count in a composition that remains visually organized.

coins-ten.name: Ten of Coins
coins-ten.Scene: The Ten of Coins shows ten circular starburst coins in the suit's fullest pip composition, the ten Bolognese denari arranged in the two-column or three-two-three-two convention of Italian pip cards. The ten-coin card represents the suit at its maximum numerical expression.

coins-fante.name: Knave (Fante) of Coins
coins-fante.Scene: The Fante (Knave) of Coins appears in the double-ended Bolognese format as a jester-like figure in colorful hat and costume, holding coins on each side. The double-ended composition means the figure is visible right-side-up from both directions, a convention that distinguishes Bolognese court cards from the single-direction Marseille courts. The knave holds the suit's circular coin emblem.

coins-cavallo.name: Knight (Cavallo) of Coins
coins-cavallo.Scene: The Cavallo (Knight) of Coins appears in the double-ended Bolognese format as a bust of a bearded or distinguished figure in colorful Renaissance doublet, holding a coin in each raised hand. The Bolognese Cavallo is shown as a bust rather than a mounted horseman, the knight's rank expressed through the doubled bust format characteristic of the tarocchino court cards.

coins-regina.name: Queen (Regina) of Coins
coins-regina.Scene: The Regina (Queen) of Coins appears in the double-ended Bolognese format. The queen figure in colorful court dress holds or displays the coin emblem, her doubled bust occupying both halves of the card. In the Italian-suited Bolognese deck the queen is the third court rank above knave and knight but below king.

coins-re.name: King (Re) of Coins
coins-re.Scene: The Re (King) of Coins appears in the double-ended Bolognese format. The king of the coins suit is the highest court rank, his figure in regal costume holding the suit's circular coin emblem doubled across the card's two halves. The Bolognese king of coins embodies the suit's material authority in the doubled format.

cups-ace.name: Ace of Cups
cups-ace.Scene: The Ace of Cups (Coppe) shows a single large ornate chalice or vase with a decorated stem and base, flanked by laurel or olive branches. A crown or crest tops the vessel, and the overall composition is heraldic — the ace of cups as an emblem of the suit's essential receptive form. In some Bolognese decks the ace of cups bears a maker's mark or civic emblem within the cup.

cups-six.name: Six of Cups
cups-six.Scene: The Six of Cups shows six cylindrical cup or chalice shapes in the Italian pip convention. The cups are rendered as tall rounded vessels in red and blue tones, arranged in columns or rows against a white background. The six-cup card is balanced and open, the suit's cylindrical emblem repeated six times in the clean Bolognese pip style.

cups-seven.name: Seven of Cups
cups-seven.Scene: The Seven of Cups shows seven cylindrical chalice shapes in the Italian pip arrangement. The cups are tall and distinctively Italian in profile — cylindrical rather than the goblet shapes of northern European decks — arranged in the slightly asymmetric pattern of odd-number pip cards. The seven cups in red and blue fill the card with the suit's characteristic vertical vessel forms.

cups-eight.name: Eight of Cups
cups-eight.Scene: The Eight of Cups shows eight cylindrical cup shapes in a symmetrical arrangement, the even number allowing a balanced two-column distribution. The eight Bolognese cups continue the suit's characteristic Italian chalice form in a composition that is dense but organized.

cups-nine.name: Nine of Cups
cups-nine.Scene: The Nine of Cups shows nine cylindrical cup shapes approaching the density of the ten. The nine cups are arranged in the Italian pip convention, the suit's chalice forms filling the card's field as the count approaches its maximum.

cups-ten.name: Ten of Cups
cups-ten.Scene: The Ten of Cups shows ten cylindrical cup shapes in the suit's fullest pip composition. Ten Bolognese chalice forms are arranged in the conventional Italian pip distribution, the ten-cup card representing the suit at its maximum numerical expression — emotional completeness in the cylindrical vessel form.

cups-fante.name: Knave (Fante) of Cups
cups-fante.Scene: The Fante (Knave) of Cups appears in the double-ended Bolognese format as a young figure in colorful plumed hat and doublet, holding cups. The cup shapes are visible in each hand of the doubled figure. The knave is the suit's youngest court member, his youthful costume and double-ended format marking him as a page of the emotional suit.

cups-cavallo.name: Knight (Cavallo) of Cups
cups-cavallo.Scene: The Cavallo (Knight) of Cups appears in the double-ended Bolognese format as a bust of a figure in colorful Renaissance costume, holding or displaying cups in each doubled half of the card. The knight of the cups suit embodies the suit's active emotional qualities in the Bolognese bust convention.

cups-regina.name: Queen (Regina) of Cups
cups-regina.Scene: The Regina (Queen) of Cups appears in the double-ended Bolognese format, her bust in court dress occupying both halves of the card. The queen of cups is the suit's feminine court authority, her doubled form characteristic of the tarocchino's treatment of all court ranks.

cups-re.name: King (Re) of Cups
cups-re.Scene: The Re (King) of Cups appears in the double-ended Bolognese format as the suit's highest court rank. The king's bust in regal costume occupies both halves of the card, holding or associated with the cup emblem. The king of cups in the tarocchino holds the suit's emotional authority in the doubled format.

swords-ace.name: Ace of Swords
swords-ace.Scene: The Ace of Swords (Spade) in the Bolognese deck is among the most ornate of the suit aces. Two large concentric rings decorated in alternating blue and red are flanked by laurel branches, with a central sword or cross shape visible between them and a crown or crest above. The overall composition is heraldic — the ace of swords as a civic or military emblem rather than a simple pip card.

swords-six.name: Six of Swords
swords-six.Scene: The Six of Swords shows six sword shapes arranged in the Italian pip convention. The Bolognese spade are shown as straight or slightly curved blades with crossguards, arranged in symmetrical crossing patterns. Six swords fill the card in the characteristic Bolognese sword pip style, which differs from both the Marseille linear arrangement and the curved-saber style of some Italian decks.

swords-seven.name: Seven of Swords
swords-seven.Scene: The Seven of Swords shows seven sword shapes in the Italian pip convention, their blades and crossguards distributed in the slightly asymmetric pattern of an odd-number pip. The seven Bolognese spade are arranged with the characteristic interlocking or crossing formation of the Italian sword pip style.

swords-eight.name: Eight of Swords
swords-eight.Scene: The Eight of Swords shows eight sword shapes in a symmetrical arrangement, the even number allowing a balanced distribution of the Bolognese spade. Eight blades in crossing or parallel formation fill the card's field in the Italian pip convention.

swords-nine.name: Nine of Swords
swords-nine.Scene: The Nine of Swords shows nine sword shapes approaching the density of the ten. Nine Bolognese spade are distributed across the card in the Italian pip convention, the suit's blade forms filling the field as the count nears its maximum.

swords-ten.name: Ten of Swords
swords-ten.Scene: The Ten of Swords shows ten sword shapes in a dense crossing pattern characteristic of the Bolognese spade pip. The Italian-style swords — straight blades with prominent crossguards — are arranged in an interlocking star or cross formation with decorative shield or node shapes at the intersections. The ten-sword card is the suit's most densely packed pip composition, the blades filling the card's field in a complex crossing pattern.

swords-fante.name: Knave (Fante) of Swords
swords-fante.Scene: The Fante (Knave) of Swords appears in the double-ended Bolognese format as a young figure in colorful Renaissance costume, holding a sword. The doubled format shows the figure in both orientations. The knave of swords holds the suit's blade as his attribute, the page of discernment and precision in the tarocchino's court hierarchy.

swords-cavallo.name: Knight (Cavallo) of Swords
swords-cavallo.Scene: The Cavallo (Knight) of Swords appears in the double-ended Bolognese format as a bust of a figure in colorful costume, holding curved swords or sabers. The doubled bust convention of the Bolognese cavallo replaces the mounted knight of other traditions with a facing portrait, the knight's rank expressed through doubling rather than through equestrian display.

swords-regina.name: Queen (Regina) of Swords
swords-regina.Scene: The Regina (Queen) of Swords appears in the double-ended Bolognese format, the queen's bust in court dress occupying both halves of the card. The queen of swords holds her blade or is associated with the suit emblem in the tarocchino's double-ended format.

swords-re.name: King (Re) of Swords
swords-re.Scene: The Re (King) of Swords appears in the double-ended Bolognese format as the suit's highest court rank. The king's bust in regal costume occupies both halves of the card, associated with the sword emblem of the suit. The king of swords in the tarocchino holds judicial and intellectual authority in the doubled format.

batons-ace.name: Ace of Batons
batons-ace.Scene: The Ace of Batons (Bastoni) in the Bolognese deck is an ornate vertical composition — a central baton flanked by laurel branches and star-shaped decorations, with a heraldic crest or emblem at top. The overall arrangement is heraldic and symmetrical, the ace of batons as a civic or guild emblem rather than a simple pip card.

batons-six.name: Six of Batons
batons-six.Scene: The Six of Batons shows six baton shapes in the Italian pip convention. The Bolognese bastoni are cylindrical staves in red and blue, arranged in a symmetrical crossing or parallel formation. The six-baton card is balanced and organized, the suit's cylindrical forms in their equitable mid-range arrangement.

batons-seven.name: Seven of Batons
batons-seven.Scene: The Seven of Batons shows seven blue, red, and yellow cylindrical baton shapes crossing in a diamond or star formation. The crossing pattern creates a central focal point where the seven bastoni intersect, their alternating blue and red stripes giving the composition a vivid color contrast. The seven-baton card is one of the most visually dynamic of the suit's pip cards.

batons-eight.name: Eight of Batons
batons-eight.Scene: The Eight of Batons shows eight cylindrical baton shapes in a symmetrical arrangement, the even number allowing a balanced geometric formation. The eight bastoni with their red, blue, and yellow stripes fill the card in the Italian pip convention with the suit's characteristic strong color contrast.

batons-nine.name: Nine of Batons
batons-nine.Scene: The Nine of Batons shows nine cylindrical baton shapes approaching the density of the ten. Nine bastoni are distributed across the card in the Italian pip convention, the suit's force accumulating toward its maximum expression.

batons-ten.name: Ten of Batons
batons-ten.Scene: The Ten of Batons shows ten cylindrical baton shapes in the suit's fullest pip composition. The ten bastoni are arranged in the densest Italian pip formation, filling the card's field with the suit's characteristic striped cylindrical forms. The ten-baton card is the suit's most loaded pip, creative energy accumulated to its maximum.

batons-fante.name: Knave (Fante) of Batons
batons-fante.Scene: The Fante (Knave) of Batons appears in the double-ended Bolognese format as a young figure in a colorful feathered hat and court costume, holding a baton. The doubled figure in two orientations carries the suit's staff as his primary attribute. The knave of batons is the suit's youngest court rank in the tarocchino's double-ended format.

batons-cavallo.name: Knight (Cavallo) of Batons
batons-cavallo.Scene: The Cavallo (Knight) of Batons appears in the double-ended Bolognese format as a bust of a figure in feathered hat and colorful costume, holding batons. The doubled bust convention places the knight of batons in the Bolognese facing-portrait format rather than the mounted posture of other traditions.

batons-regina.name: Queen (Regina) of Batons
batons-regina.Scene: The Regina (Queen) of Batons appears in the double-ended Bolognese format, her bust in colorful court dress occupying both halves of the card. The queen of batons holds or is associated with the suit's baton emblem in the tarocchino's doubled court format.

batons-re.name: King (Re) of Batons
batons-re.Scene: The Re (King) of Batons appears in the double-ended Bolognese format as the suit's highest court rank. The king's doubled bust in regal costume carries the baton emblem and represents the suit's ultimate creative and civic authority in the tarocchino's double-ended format.

emg-papi.name: The Four Papi — the Bolognese Signature
emg-papi.Scene: The four Papi Mori — the Bolognese Moorish substitutes for trumps II through V — are grouped together as the deck's most historically distinctive feature. These four secular figures in colorful court dress replaced the Papessa, Empress, Emperor, and Pope in 18th-century Bologna, a substitution attributed variously to religious caution and to civic regulations on card imagery. Each figure holds a lance and is rendered in the double-ended Bolognese format.

emg-trumps.name: The Trumps in the Bolognese Order
emg-trumps.Scene: The twenty-two trumps of the Tarocchino Bolognese ordered in the Bolognese sequence: Matto (Fool), Bagatto (I), the four Papi (II-V), Amore (VI), Carro (VII), Temperanza (VIII), Giustizia (VIIII), Forza (X), Ruota (XI), Vecchio (XII), Traditore (XIII), Morte (XIIII), Diavolo (XV), Torre (XVI), Stella (XVII), Luna (XVIII), Sole (XVIIII), Mondo (XX), Angelo (XXI). The Bolognese order places Mondo before Angelo, reversing the standard sequence.

emg-suit-coins.name: Suit of Coins (Denari) — pips 2–5 removed
emg-suit-coins.Scene: The suit of Coins (Denari) in the Tarocchino Bolognese includes the Ace plus six through ten (pips two through five having been removed), plus the four court ranks: Fante, Cavallo, Regina, Re. The starburst circular coins of the Italian Denari suit are displayed in clean pip arrangements. The suit's ace carries the manufacturer's cartouche in the Bolognese tradition.

emg-suit-cups.name: Suit of Cups (Coppe) — pips 2–5 removed
emg-suit-cups.Scene: The suit of Cups (Coppe) in the Tarocchino Bolognese includes the Ace plus six through ten plus the four courts. The cylindrical Italian chalice forms of the Bolognese coppe are distinctive — taller and more geometric than the goblet shapes of northern European decks. The cups suit's ace bears the suit's heraldic chalice emblem in ornate form.

emg-suit-swords.name: Suit of Swords (Spade) — pips 2–5 removed
emg-suit-swords.Scene: The suit of Swords (Spade) in the Tarocchino Bolognese includes the Ace plus six through ten plus the four courts. The straight-bladed Italian swords of the Bolognese spade are arranged in crossing patterns with decorative shield-nodes at the intersections. The ace bears the suit's distinctive heraldic ring composition.

emg-suit-batons.name: Suit of Batons (Bastoni) — pips 2–5 removed
emg-suit-batons.Scene: The suit of Batons (Bastoni) in the Tarocchino Bolognese includes the Ace plus six through ten plus the four courts. The striped cylindrical bastoni of the Bolognese tradition are arranged in crossing and diamond formations. The ace bears the suit's heraldic staff emblem with flanking laurel branches.

kw-pip.name: Pip
kw-pip.Scene: Pip cards in the Tarocchino Bolognese are the numbered non-court suit cards: Ace plus six through ten in each suit (pips two through five having been removed). The pip range is thus: Ace, Six, Seven, Eight, Nine, Ten — six pip cards per suit rather than the ten of a standard tarot deck. This abbreviated pip range is the defining structural feature of the tarocchino game format.

kw-bolognese.name: Bolognese
kw-bolognese.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all items identified with the Bolognese tradition — the regional Italian tarot variant that developed in Bologna from the 15th century onward, becoming the Tarocchino game. The Bolognese tradition is characterized by the removal of lower pip cards, the substitution of four Moors for the early trumps, the double-ended court format, and a trump ordering distinct from Marseille.

kw-tarocchino.name: Tarocchino
kw-tarocchino.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all items identified as belonging to the Tarocchino — the specifically Bolognese game format using a 62-card deck (78 cards minus the 2-5 pips from each suit). The tarocchino remained in active play in Bologna into the 20th century, one of the longest-surviving regional tarot game traditions in Europe.

kw-trionfi.name: Trionfi
kw-trionfi.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all trump items identified with the Trionfi tradition — the Italian allegorical sequence of triumphs that forms the conceptual basis of tarot's major arcana. The Bolognese Trionfi follow the sequence of Petrarchan allegorical victories: Love, Chastity, Death, Fame, Time, Eternity — though the specific Bolognese order reflects local adaptations.

kw-court.name: Court
kw-court.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all court cards in the Tarocchino Bolognese: Fante, Cavallo, Regina, and Re across all four suits. The Bolognese courts are distinctive for their double-ended format and their use of bust or half-figure compositions rather than the full-figure upright presentations of Marseille-tradition decks.

kw-air.name: Air
kw-air.Scene: A keyword axis grouping items associated with the element Air in the Bolognese tarot — conventionally the suit of Swords (Spade), associated with the intellect, communication, and the mental faculties. In the Italian elemental correspondence the sword's cutting quality is linked to the swift and penetrating nature of air.

kw-bastoni.name: Bastoni
kw-bastoni.Scene: A keyword axis using the Italian name for the suit of Batons — Bastoni — grouping all items identified with this suit in the Bolognese tarocchino.

kw-batons.name: Batons
kw-batons.Scene: A keyword axis using the English name for the suit of Batons, grouping all items identified with this suit across the deck's items.

kw-coins.name: Coins
kw-coins.Scene: A keyword axis using the English name for the suit of Coins (Denari), grouping all items identified with this suit across the deck's items.

kw-coppe.name: Coppe
kw-coppe.Scene: A keyword axis using the Italian name for the suit of Cups — Coppe — grouping all items identified with this suit in the Bolognese tarocchino.

kw-cups.name: Cups
kw-cups.Scene: A keyword axis using the English name for the suit of Cups, grouping all items identified with this suit across the deck's items.

kw-denari.name: Denari
kw-denari.Scene: A keyword axis using the Italian name for the suit of Coins — Denari — grouping all items identified with this suit in the Bolognese tarocchino.

kw-earth.name: Earth
kw-earth.Scene: A keyword axis grouping items associated with the element Earth in the Bolognese tarot — conventionally the suit of Coins (Denari), linked to material substance, stability, and the tangible world. The circular coin's solidity and its association with land and physical wealth makes it the earth suit in elemental correspondence.

kw-fire.name: Fire
kw-fire.Scene: A keyword axis grouping items associated with the element Fire in the Bolognese tarot — conventionally the suit of Batons (Bastoni), linked to creative energy, enterprise, and the generative spark. The baton or wand's association with action, growth, and ardor makes it the fire suit in elemental correspondence.

kw-spade.name: Spade
kw-spade.Scene: A keyword axis using the Italian name for the suit of Swords — Spade — grouping all items identified with this suit in the Bolognese tarocchino.

kw-swords.name: Swords
kw-swords.Scene: A keyword axis using the English name for the suit of Swords, grouping all items identified with this suit across the deck's items.

kw-water.name: Water
kw-water.Scene: A keyword axis grouping items associated with the element Water in the Bolognese tarot — conventionally the suit of Cups (Coppe), linked to emotion, intuition, and the fluid inner life. The cup's receptive, containing quality and its association with feeling and imagination makes it the water suit in elemental correspondence.

kw-ace.name: Ace
kw-ace.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all four Ace cards — one per suit — in the Tarocchino Bolognese. The aces (Ace of Coins, Cups, Swords, Batons) are the suit-foundation cards, each marked with the manufacturer's emblem in the Bolognese tradition. The aces begin the truncated pip sequence (Ace, Six through Ten) of the tarocchino.

kw-cavallo.name: Cavallo
kw-cavallo.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all four Cavallo (Knight) cards — one per suit — in the Tarocchino Bolognese. The cavalli are the second court rank in the Italian four-court system (Fante/Cavallo/Regina/Re), rendered as double-ended busts in the Bolognese format rather than as mounted horsemen.

kw-eight.name: Eight
kw-eight.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all Eight pip cards across the four suits of the tarocchino. The eights (Eight of Coins, Cups, Swords, Batons) represent the suit at its stable mid-to-upper range — in the abbreviated Bolognese sequence that omits pips two through five, the eight sits near the high end of the pip range.

kw-fante.name: Fante
kw-fante.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all four Fante (Knave/Page) cards — one per suit — in the Tarocchino Bolognese. The fanti are the lowest court rank in the Italian four-court system, rendered as double-ended figures in the Bolognese format. Each fante carries the emblem of their suit in a youthful and colorful costume.

kw-nine.name: Nine
kw-nine.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all Nine pip cards across the four suits of the tarocchino. The nines (Nine of Coins, Cups, Swords, Batons) represent the suit approaching its maximum pip count — one step from the ten in the abbreviated Bolognese sequence that runs Ace, Six through Ten.

kw-papa-moro.name: Papa / moro
kw-papa-moro.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all four Papa Moro cards — the Bolognese Moorish substitutes for trumps II through V. The term 'Papa Moro' (Moorish Pope) reflects the Bolognese naming of these secular substitute figures who replaced the Papessa, Empress, Emperor, and Pope. Each figure holds a lance and is distinguished by slight variations in costume and headgear.

kw-re.name: Re
kw-re.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all four Re (King) cards — one per suit — in the Tarocchino Bolognese. The re are the highest court rank in the Italian four-court system, rendered as double-ended busts in colorful regal costumes. Each king holds or is associated with the emblem of his suit.

kw-regina.name: Regina
kw-regina.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all four Regina (Queen) cards — one per suit — in the Tarocchino Bolognese. The regine are the third court rank in the Italian system (below king, above knight), rendered as double-ended busts in court dress. The inclusion of a queen rather than a second male court rank reflects the Italian four-court system's feminine third rank.

kw-seven.name: Seven
kw-seven.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all Seven pip cards across the four suits of the tarocchino. The sevens (Seven of Coins, Cups, Swords, Batons) represent the suit in its active mid-range — in the abbreviated Bolognese sequence the seven sits in the lower-middle of the pip range (Ace, Six, Seven, Eight, Nine, Ten).

kw-six.name: Six
kw-six.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all Six pip cards across the four suits of the tarocchino. The sixes (Six of Coins, Cups, Swords, Batons) are the lowest numbered pips in the Bolognese abbreviated sequence — the first step above the Ace in a deck from which pips two through five have been removed.

kw-ten.name: Ten
kw-ten.Scene: A keyword axis grouping all Ten pip cards across the four suits of the tarocchino. The tens (Ten of Coins, Cups, Swords, Batons) are the highest numbered pips in the Bolognese abbreviated sequence, representing each suit at its fullest pip expression before the court cards begin.

axis-keyword.name: By Keyword
axis-keyword.Scene: A navigational axis organizing all items in the Tarocchino Bolognese by keyword — grouping suits, pip values, court ranks, and special features (the Papi Mori, elemental associations, Italian vs. English names) into a cross-cutting structure. The keyword axis allows navigation across the deck by thematic category rather than by suit or trump sequence.
